title: The Urban Water Cycle as a Planning Tool to Monitor SARS-CoV-2: A Review of the Literature

subsections.subsection_title: Virological and Epidemiological Foundations of COVID-19
subsections.content:
COVID-19 is caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), an enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA betacoronavirus genetically related to SARS-CoV and other zoonotic coronaviruses ref [4]. Its biological profile is epidemiologically important because high viral replication in the upper respiratory tract can occur around, or even before, symptom onset, enabling efficient community transmission and complicating case-based containment ref [1], ref [3]. Clinical expression ranges from asymptomatic infection to severe pneumonia and multisystem disease, which means that reported cases capture only part of the true infection burden.

Early outbreak investigations in Wuhan established sustained human-to-human transmission and showed rapid epidemic growth, with short doubling times and substantial infection exportation before stringent controls were implemented ref [1], ref [3]. Initial estimates of the basic reproductive number generally exceeded 2, and some comparative analyses suggested that SARS-CoV-2 was more transmissible than the 2003 SARS coronavirus ref [2], ref [3]. These epidemiological features, combined with heterogeneous symptom severity and delays between infection, testing, and reporting, created major challenges for timely surveillance and risk assessment.

For urban monitoring, the key implication is that infection dynamics are only imperfectly represented by clinical surveillance. The presence of presymptomatic, paucisymptomatic, and unreported infections broadens the gap between true incidence and notified cases, while viral shedding through feces introduces an additional population-level signal relevant to environmental surveillance. Accordingly, understanding the virological and epidemiological foundations of COVID-19 provides the conceptual basis for integrating wastewater observations into urban public health planning.

SARS-CoV-2 is transmitted predominantly through respiratory particles generated during breathing, speaking, coughing, and sneezing, with both short-range droplet exposure and inhalation of finer aerosols contributing to infection risk. Early reports also highlighted transmission from presymptomatic or asymptomatic individuals, which complicated case detection and amplified community spread before symptom-based interventions could be deployed effectively ref [7], ref [4], ref [5]. These features are especially relevant for urban settings, where crowding, mobility, and shared indoor environments increase opportunities for repeated exposure.

Beyond the respiratory tract, gastrointestinal involvement has important environmental implications. Viral RNA and, in some cases, infectious virus have been detected in feces, and evidence of gastrointestinal infection indicates that enteric shedding may persist even after respiratory samples become negative ref [6], ref [6], ref [7]. This does not establish fecal-oral transmission as a dominant route, but it does provide the biological basis for viral loading into sewer networks and supports wastewater surveillance as a population-level monitoring approach.

Environmental persistence further shapes indirect exposure pathways and interpretation of water-cycle signals. Experimental and review evidence shows that human coronaviruses, including SARS-CoV-2, can remain viable on inanimate surfaces from hours to days depending on material type, temperature, humidity, and initial inoculum, while common disinfectants are generally effective at inactivation ref [5], ref [8]. In aerosols, SARS-CoV-2 can also retain infectivity for several hours under laboratory conditions ref [9]. In water and wastewater matrices, detectable RNA often persists longer than infectious virus, so measured signals more reliably indicate community shedding than direct environmental infectivity; this distinction is central when translating wastewater detections into public-health interpretation ref [10].

subsections.subsection_title: Contextual Drivers of Spread and Population Vulnerability
subsections.content:
Beyond intrinsic viral properties, COVID-19 transmission is shaped by contextual drivers operating at multiple scales, including climate, mobility, housing, occupation, and the timing and stringency of nonpharmaceutical interventions. Comparative analyses across Chinese cities showed that meteorological conditions influenced local transmissibility, but their effects were strongly conditioned by public health measures, underscoring that environmental factors modulate rather than determine epidemic dynamics ref [8]. Broader epidemiological syntheses likewise indicate that crowding, prolonged indoor contact, and unequal capacity to reduce mobility are central determinants of heterogeneous spread across urban settings ref [3], ref [4].

Population vulnerability is similarly patterned by social and spatial inequality. Individuals experiencing homelessness face elevated exposure risks because of congregate shelters, limited access to hygiene and sanitation, high burdens of chronic illness, and barriers to testing and isolation ref [9]. Comparable vulnerabilities have been documented among residents of informal settlements and densely populated low-income neighborhoods, where overcrowding, intermittent water access, and dependence on shared sanitation can hinder infection prevention and amplify indirect impacts of the pandemic ref [5], ref [6]. Age, comorbidity, and occupational exposure further interact with these structural conditions to concentrate severe outcomes in already disadvantaged groups ref [7], ref [8].

For an urban water-cycle perspective, these contextual drivers matter because wastewater signals are generated within socially differentiated populations. Variations in sewer connectivity, per-capita water use, institutionalized settings, and the presence of underserved groups can affect who is represented in wastewater surveillance and how signals should be interpreted. Thus, wastewater-based epidemiology is most informative when integrated with demographic, infrastructural, and vulnerability data, allowing planners to distinguish true infection trends from artifacts of uneven service access or population composition ref [6], ref [9].

subsections.subsection_title: Urban Water Cycle and Wastewater-Based Perspectives
subsections.content:
The urban water cycle provides a systems-level lens for understanding how SARS-CoV-2 signals move through households, sewers, wastewater treatment plants, sludge streams, and, in some settings, receiving waters or reused water pathways. Early water-sector commentaries emphasized that the pandemic should be interpreted not only as a clinical and respiratory crisis but also as an urban infrastructure challenge, because viral RNA shed in feces and other excreta can enter sewered and non-sewered sanitation networks and create measurable community-level signatures ref [10], ref [11]. This framing links epidemiology with urban metabolism and highlights the need to consider inequalities in sanitation coverage, sewer connectivity, and treatment performance when assessing both surveillance opportunities and residual environmental risks ref [10], ref [13].

Within this framework, wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) emerged as a practical population-scale monitoring tool. Detection of SARS-CoV-2 RNA in municipal wastewater was rapidly demonstrated across diverse contexts, including early proof-of-concept work in India, showing that wastewater surveillance could reveal circulation of the virus independent of individual clinical testing ref [12]. Subsequent work argued that wastewater data can provide temporally integrated information on infection dynamics, potentially capturing asymptomatic and pre-symptomatic shedding and offering an early warning signal for outbreaks or resurgences ref [11], ref [13]. For urban planning, this makes WBE valuable not only for public-health response but also for identifying underserved catchments, prioritizing targeted testing, and supporting adaptive management of critical water infrastructure.

At the same time, wastewater perspectives require careful interpretation. RNA detection does not by itself demonstrate infectivity, and risk assessment must distinguish between molecular surveillance utility and actual transmission hazards in sewage, treatment trains, biosolids, and downstream waters ref [11], ref [13]. Sampling design, sewer travel time, dilution, industrial inputs, stormwater intrusion, and decentralized sanitation can all affect signal strength and comparability across cities ref [10], ref [13]. Accordingly, the urban water cycle should be viewed as both a monitoring platform and a planning framework: it enables spatially resolved surveillance while also revealing where infrastructure deficits, exposure pathways, and governance gaps may amplify vulnerability during pandemics ref [10], ref [11], ref [13].

subsections.subsection_title: Clinical and Epidemiological Characteristics of COVID-19
subsections.content:
COVID-19 presents with a broad clinical spectrum, ranging from asymptomatic infection to severe viral pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome, multiorgan dysfunction, and death. Early cohort studies established that fever, cough, fatigue, and dyspnea are the dominant presenting features, while disease severity increases with older age, male sex, and comorbidities such as hypertension, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease ref [14], ref [3], ref [4]. Population-based analyses also showed marked heterogeneity in transmission and outcomes across settings, with presymptomatic and mildly symptomatic individuals contributing substantially to community spread ref [14], ref [5].

From an epidemiological perspective, the incubation period is typically around 5 days, and the serial interval can be sufficiently short to permit transmission before symptom onset, complicating case-based control strategies ref [5], ref [6]. Virological studies demonstrated high viral loads in the upper respiratory tract near the time of presentation, including in patients with mild disease, which helps explain efficient person-to-person spread and the rapid establishment of outbreaks in dense urban environments ref [7]. These features are particularly relevant to urban water-cycle surveillance because wastewater signals may integrate contributions from clinically apparent, pauci-symptomatic, and undiagnosed infections that are missed by routine testing.

Although respiratory manifestations define the syndrome, extrapulmonary involvement is common and clinically important. Reviews of hospitalized cohorts reported that gastrointestinal symptoms, liver enzyme abnormalities, and other systemic manifestations occur in a meaningful subset of patients, reinforcing that COVID-19 is not solely a respiratory infection ref [15], ref [8]. This broader clinical phenotype, together with variation in symptom onset, severity, and healthcare-seeking behavior, underpins the value of complementary surveillance approaches such as wastewater-based epidemiology for tracking infection dynamics at population scale.

subsections.subsection_title: Gastrointestinal Involvement and Fecal Viral Shedding
subsections.content:
Beyond its respiratory presentation, COVID-19 frequently involves the gastrointestinal tract. Reported symptoms include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and loss of appetite, with prevalence varying across cohorts and disease stages ref [16], ref [3], ref [4]. Mechanistically, this tropism is biologically plausible because ACE2, the principal host receptor for SARS-CoV-2, is highly expressed in enterocytes and other digestive tract tissues, supporting direct intestinal infection and replication ref [16], ref [5].

A consistent implication of gastrointestinal involvement is fecal viral shedding. Multiple clinical studies detected SARS-CoV-2 RNA in stool or anal/rectal swabs of infected patients, including individuals with and without overt digestive symptoms ref [17], ref [6], ref [7]. Importantly, fecal RNA shedding often persists after respiratory samples become negative, indicating that the gastrointestinal tract may remain a longer-lasting compartment of viral excretion ref [17], ref [6], ref [8]. This temporal decoupling is particularly relevant for environmental surveillance because wastewater signals may integrate infections that are no longer captured by respiratory testing alone.

For urban water cycle monitoring, the key epidemiological consequence is that sewered wastewater can contain viral RNA from a broad spectrum of infected individuals, including pre-symptomatic, mildly symptomatic, and convalescent cases ref [17], ref [7], ref [8]. However, RNA detection in feces does not necessarily imply the routine presence of infectious virus, and the extent of fecal-oral transmission remains uncertain ref [4], ref [9]. Thus, the strongest current value of fecal shedding evidence lies in supporting wastewater-based epidemiology as a population-level surveillance tool rather than as proof of waterborne transmission risk.

subsections.subsection_title: Wastewater Surveillance Methods and System Implications
subsections.content:
Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) has emerged as a practical complement to clinical testing because SARS-CoV-2 RNA can be detected in municipal sewage before or alongside increases in reported cases, providing population-level early warning. Policy-oriented accounts from the UK emphasized sewer monitoring as a near-real-time public health defense, while broader assessments of wastewater utility operations highlighted WBE as both a surveillance tool and a management challenge during the pandemic ref [4], ref [18]. This framing is especially relevant in urban planning contexts, where sewersheds offer spatially resolved signals that can support targeted interventions.

Methodologically, surveillance sensitivity depends on sampling strategy, concentration, extraction, and molecular detection. Composite influent samples are generally preferred over grab samples because they better integrate diurnal variability, whereas upstream building- or neighborhood-scale sampling can improve spatial specificity at the cost of greater hydraulic uncertainty. Among concentration workflows, polyethylene glycol precipitation followed by acid guanidinium thiocyanate-phenol-chloroform extraction has been shown to be applicable for recovering SARS-CoV-2 RNA from municipal wastewater, illustrating the importance of method standardization and recovery control selection ref [20]. Metagenomic analyses further demonstrate that wastewater influent contains complex viral and microbial backgrounds, underscoring why targeted RT-qPCR or RT-dPCR assays remain central for routine SARS-CoV-2 quantification while sequencing is valuable for variant and community profiling ref [19], ref [5].

System implications extend beyond analytics. Viral RNA measurements are shaped by sewer travel time, dilution from stormwater or industrial inputs, solids partitioning, and decay during conveyance, which complicate back-calculation from concentration to infection prevalence ref [18], ref [6]. At treatment plants, current evidence indicates that conventional treatment substantially reduces viral RNA and infectious risk, yet the pandemic exposed needs for operator protection, resilient monitoring infrastructure, and integration of wastewater data with epidemiological dashboards ref [18], ref [7]. Taken together, these studies position the urban water cycle not merely as a passive recipient of viral shedding, but as an operational sensing network for public health surveillance.

subsections.section_title: Monitoring Across Urban Water Cycle Components
subsections.content:
Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) in sewage networks rapidly emerged as a population-scale surveillance tool because SARS-CoV-2 RNA can be detected in municipal influent before, and sometimes independently of, case reporting. Early evidence from the Netherlands showed that viral RNA was measurable in sewage during the initial epidemic phase and tracked reported prevalence, establishing the feasibility of sewer-based monitoring for community transmission assessment ref [21]. Subsequent studies from India and the United States confirmed detection across diverse sewered settings, demonstrating that sewage surveillance could reveal persistent circulation during both growth and post-lockdown phases ref [22], ref [12], ref [24], ref [28].

At the network scale, WBE offers several planning advantages: it aggregates contributions from symptomatic and asymptomatic shedders, provides geographically resolved trend information when sampling is distributed across interceptor lines or treatment plant catchments, and can support early warning of outbreak resurgence ref [23], ref [26]. However, interpretation remains sensitive to sewer hydraulics, travel time, dilution by industrial flows or stormwater, sampling design, and laboratory recovery efficiency. Reviews and collaborative initiatives emphasized the need for harmonized protocols spanning composite sampling, concentration methods, molecular assays, and metadata reporting to improve comparability across jurisdictions ref [23], ref [25].

A central question for operational deployment is detection sensitivity at low prevalence. Modeling work estimating the minimum number of infected individuals needed for reliable wastewater detection showed that observability depends strongly on fecal shedding variability, catchment size, and analytical limits of detection ref [27]. Accordingly, sewage-network WBE is most powerful as a trend and sentinel system rather than a direct substitute for clinical incidence, and it is best interpreted through integration with epidemiological, demographic, and sewer-system information ref [22], ref [23], ref [27].

subsections.section_title: Monitoring Across Urban Water Cycle Components
subsections.content:
Building- and campus-scale wastewater monitoring extends wastewater-based epidemiology from sewershed-level trend analysis to near-source surveillance, where viral signals can be associated with dormitories, residential blocks, or individual facilities. This scale offers greater spatial resolution and faster operational feedback, making it attractive for outbreak detection in congregate settings such as university housing. A non-intrusive residential-building study showed that building outflows could be sampled without major plumbing modifications and that SARS-CoV-2 RNA measurements tracked known case occurrence, illustrating the feasibility of localized monitoring under real occupancy conditions ref [29]. Similarly, campus implementations demonstrated that building-level wastewater surveillance can be integrated into public-health workflows to prioritize diagnostic testing and support targeted intervention strategies ref [30].

The main strength of building-scale monitoring is actionability: compared with municipal influent, positive detections can trigger focused clinical testing, isolation guidance, or intensified cleaning in a much narrower population pool ref [29], ref [30]. However, this increased granularity comes with methodological challenges. Small contributing populations produce intermittent fecal inputs, stronger dilution effects from graywater, and greater sensitivity to sampling timing and hydraulic variability. As a result, composite sampling, careful site selection, and knowledge of internal plumbing and occupancy patterns become especially important for interpreting non-detects and short-term fluctuations ref [29], ref [30].

From a planning perspective, campus wastewater programs function best when embedded in a broader surveillance architecture that links environmental measurements to case reporting, testing logistics, and decision thresholds. The university-campus literature emphasizes that implementation requires coordination across facilities management, laboratories, and health services, as well as clear protocols for escalation after positive signals ref [30]. Thus, building- and campus-scale wastewater monitoring is not simply a higher-resolution version of sewer surveillance; it is a distinct operational layer within the urban water cycle, best suited to semi-closed communities where rapid, localized response is feasible ref [29], ref [30].

subsections.section_title: Monitoring Across Urban Water Cycle Components
subsections.subsection_title: Environmental Waters, Surface Persistence, and Exposure Pathways
subsections.content:
Beyond sewer networks, SARS-CoV-2 monitoring has been extended to environmental waters, particularly rivers receiving untreated or insufficiently treated wastewater. This pathway is most consequential in low-sanitation settings, where direct sewage discharge can make river water a proxy for community infection trends while also raising concerns about downstream exposure [4]. Reviews of recreational and ambient waters likewise frame these systems less as confirmed major transmission routes and more as vulnerable interfaces where fecal contamination, hydrological dilution, and local sanitation infrastructure jointly determine detectable viral signals and public-health relevance [2].

Current evidence suggests that detection of viral RNA in environmental waters does not by itself imply infectious risk. The main exposure pathways discussed in the literature include accidental ingestion during recreation, contact with contaminated surfaces, and inhalation of aerosols generated from wastewater or turbulent water bodies [2], [3]. However, the plausibility of viable virus transmission is constrained by dilution, sunlight, temperature, oxidants, microbial antagonism, and time in the environment, all of which tend to reduce persistence outside protected matrices [3]. Thus, environmental-water surveillance is better interpreted as a complementary indicator of fecal loading and outbreak circulation than as direct evidence of waterborne COVID-19 transmission [2], [4].

Surface persistence studies provide an important boundary condition for interpreting environmental exposure. Coronaviruses can remain detectable on inanimate surfaces from hours to days depending on material type, temperature, and humidity, but they are also susceptible to common biocidal agents [1]. Taken together, the literature supports a risk framework in which environmental waters, fomites, and aerosols represent context-dependent secondary exposure pathways requiring targeted management, especially where wastewater control is limited [1], [3], [4]. For urban water-cycle planning, this justifies integrating river monitoring, recreational-water advisories, sanitation upgrades, and surface hygiene into a multi-barrier surveillance and risk-reduction strategy.

subsections.section_title: Monitoring Across Urban Water Cycle Components
subsections.subsection_title: Fate, Transport, and System Management Across the Urban Water Cycle
subsections.content:
Across the urban water cycle, SARS-CoV-2 monitoring must be interpreted through the coupled processes of release, partitioning, dilution, decay, and hydraulic transport. Reviews of coronaviruses in wastewater emphasize that viral RNA measured in sewers reflects not only community shedding but also travel time, temperature, solids association, chemical conditions, and treatment operations, all of which can alter apparent concentrations before sampling ref [32], ref [13]. Physicochemical modeling further shows that sewer-scale measurements are shaped by flow dynamics and in-sewer transformations, supporting the use of mass-balance and transport models to rationalize temporal trends rather than treating raw concentrations as direct prevalence proxies ref [35].

System management is therefore integral to surveillance design. Plumbing and building drainage can create distinct transport and exposure pathways, including aerosolization and cross-connection risks, highlighting the need to consider hydraulic defects, ventilation, and trap integrity alongside monitoring data ref [33]. At the network and plant levels, operational changes during the pandemic affected sampling representativeness, worker protection, sludge handling, and disinfection practices, while treatment barriers generally reduce infectivity even when RNA remains detectable ref [32], ref [18]. Earlier hospital-sewage studies on SARS-CoV also showed that virus detection depends strongly on concentration methods and on-site disinfection context, underscoring the importance of harmonized protocols across system components ref [34].

Taken together, fate-and-transport understanding links surveillance to action: upstream building signals, sewer-network trends, and treatment-plant measurements should be interpreted as parts of one managed system. This systems perspective supports more robust normalization, better sensor placement, and operational responses that jointly reduce uncertainty in epidemiological inference and potential occupational or environmental risks ref [13], ref [18], ref [35].

subsections.section_title: Benefits, Outcomes, and Spatial Dimensions of Surveillance
subsections.subsection_title: Wastewater Surveillance as a Public Health Data Source
subsections.content:
Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) has emerged as a valuable public health data source because SARS-CoV-2 RNA shed in feces and excreta can be detected in sewer networks before, or independently of, clinical case reporting. This makes wastewater a pooled, non-invasive indicator of community infection dynamics, capable of capturing symptomatic, pre-symptomatic, and asymptomatic infections without individual testing bias. Early reviews emphasized this dual significance of wastewater as both a potential risk matrix and, more importantly for planning, a population-level surveillance medium ref [36].

Subsequent empirical studies showed that SARS-CoV-2 concentrations in influent wastewater often correlate with incident cases, hospitalizations, and epidemic trends, and in many settings provide an early-warning signal several days in advance of clinical surveillance ref [2], ref [3], ref [4]. Because signals are aggregated over sewersheds, WBE is especially useful when clinical testing access is uneven, reporting delays are substantial, or home-based testing reduces case ascertainment ref [5], ref [6]. Methodological work has also demonstrated that normalization strategies, sampling frequency, and sewer system characteristics strongly affect interpretability, reinforcing the need to treat wastewater measurements as planning data tied to specific spatial catchments rather than as direct prevalence estimates ref [4], ref [7].

From a planning perspective, the principal benefit of wastewater surveillance is its ability to support geographically resolved, near-real-time situational awareness. Building-, neighborhood-, and treatment-plant-scale monitoring can inform targeted interventions, resource allocation, and the evaluation of public health responses while preserving privacy at the individual level ref [6], ref [8]. As a result, WBE has become an important complementary data stream within urban health intelligence systems, particularly when integrated with clinical, demographic, and infrastructure data to interpret spatial heterogeneity across the urban water cycle ref [36], ref [5].

subsections.section_title: Benefits, Outcomes, and Spatial Dimensions of Surveillance
subsections.subsection_title: Environmental Transmission Risks in Wastewater Contexts
subsections.content:
Environmental transmission risks in wastewater contexts have been discussed primarily through the lens of viral persistence, aerosolization, and sanitation inequality. Reviews of SARS-CoV-2 occurrence in sewage emphasize that detection of viral RNA does not, by itself, establish infectivity; nonetheless, the presence of fecally shed virus raises concern where untreated wastewater is discharged, reused, or handled with limited protection, especially in low-resource settings with poor sewerage coverage and high human contact with contaminated water ref [37], ref [2], ref [3].

Experimental and environmental evidence suggests that enveloped coronaviruses are generally less stable than many enteric viruses, yet they can remain detectable for meaningful periods depending on temperature, solids content, and sunlight exposure ref [4], ref [5]. This makes the highest plausible risks occupational and localized: wastewater workers, informal sanitation laborers, and residents exposed to sewer overflows, open drains, or toilet plume aerosols may face greater opportunities for contact with contaminated droplets or fomites than the general public ref [37], ref [6], ref [7]. However, current assessments consistently conclude that confirmed transmission via wastewater remains unproven and likely secondary to dominant respiratory pathways ref [3], ref [8].

From a planning perspective, the environmental-risk dimension is therefore less a claim of major sewage-borne spread than a justification for precautionary management. Targeted interventions include reliable disinfection, sludge treatment, personal protective equipment for sanitation workers, and prioritization of informal settlements and decentralized systems where infrastructure deficits amplify exposure pathways ref [37], ref [2], ref [8]. In this sense, wastewater surveillance and wastewater risk management are complementary: the same urban water cycle data used for epidemiologic monitoring can also identify places where environmental exposure control is most urgently needed.

The accumulated literature strongly supports wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) as a population-level tool for tracking SARS-CoV-2 circulation. Early studies in the Netherlands detected viral RNA in sewage during the initial epidemic phase and showed correspondence with reported case prevalence, establishing proof of concept for community surveillance ref [21]. Broader public-health analyses subsequently argued that wastewater offers a complementary signal to clinical testing because it can capture both symptomatic and asymptomatic shedding, potentially providing earlier warning of transmission trends ref [38]. Similar feasibility was rapidly demonstrated in low- and middle-income settings, including India, where SARS-CoV-2 genetic material was identified in urban wastewater, reinforcing the portability of WBE across different sanitation and monitoring contexts ref [12].

Taken together, these findings indicate that the evidentiary strength of WBE lies less in exact case quantification than in trend detection, spatial comparison, and early outbreak awareness. Across settings, wastewater signals have been shown to rise with increasing community burden and to reveal infections even when clinical surveillance is limited or delayed ref [21], ref [38], ref [12]. The synthesis of current evidence therefore positions urban wastewater monitoring as a practical planning instrument: it can support situational awareness, prioritize targeted testing or intervention, and augment conventional epidemiological reporting. At the same time, the literature implies that interpretation must remain calibrated to local sewer connectivity, sampling design, and analytical capacity, so that surveillance outputs are used as robust public-health indicators rather than as stand-alone measures of absolute prevalence ref [38].

From a planning perspective, the environmental fate of SARS-CoV-2 across the urban water cycle is central to interpreting wastewater signals and to bounding public-health risk. Current evidence indicates that viral RNA can be detected in raw wastewater, sewer biofilms, sludge, and occasionally receiving waters, but RNA persistence should not be equated with infectivity. Reviews of coronaviruses in wastewater processes consistently conclude that enveloped viruses are generally less stable than many enteric viruses and are susceptible to oxidants, detergents, sunlight, temperature, and solids-associated removal during treatment ref [32], ref [11].

These fate characteristics imply that the dominant value of wastewater surveillance is epidemiological inference rather than confirmation of waterborne transmission. Sewer residence time, dilution, stormwater inputs, and adsorption to suspended solids can all alter measured concentrations before sampling, while treatment steps such as settling, biological processing, filtration, and disinfection further reduce viable virus ref [32], ref [11]. Complementary assessments of water environments have therefore emphasized that detection in environmental matrices should be interpreted alongside context-specific decay and exposure conditions, not as standalone evidence of infectious hazard ref [31], ref [32].

Transmission through recreational or ambient waters remains plausible in theory but appears to be a secondary pathway with limited empirical support compared with respiratory exposure. Risk discussions in recreational waters have highlighted uncertainty around minimum infectious dose, viability after dilution, and the strong attenuating effects of sunlight, salinity, and conventional water treatment ref [31]. Accordingly, urban-water monitoring frameworks should treat environmental surveillance as an early-warning and trend-analysis tool, while reserving direct transmission claims for settings where viability, exposure, and dose can be jointly substantiated ref [31], ref [11].

subsections.subsection_title: Supplementary Perspectives on Feasibility and Implementation
subsections.content:
From an implementation perspective, wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) is most feasible when it is embedded in existing urban water infrastructure rather than treated as a stand-alone emergency measure. Comparative assessments emphasize that the economic advantage of WBE arises from population-level coverage, especially where clinical testing is costly, delayed, or unevenly accessible; however, feasibility depends on sewer connectivity, sampling logistics, laboratory capacity, and data integration with public-health reporting systems ref [39], ref [2]. In practice, these conditions make WBE particularly attractive as a complementary surveillance layer rather than a substitute for case-based surveillance ref [3], ref [4].

Operationally, implementation requires attention to scale, representativeness, and standardization. Building-level or neighborhood monitoring can support targeted interventions, but signal interpretation becomes sensitive to variable occupancy, flow dilution, industrial inputs, and stormwater infiltration. At larger catchment scales, surveillance is more stable but less spatially precise. Interlaboratory studies and methodological reviews have shown that harmonized protocols for sampling frequency, concentration, normalization, and quality assurance are essential if trends are to be compared across sites and over time ref [5], ref [6], ref [7]. These requirements also affect equity, since low-resource settings may benefit from sentinel sampling strategies but face constraints in cold-chain management, molecular testing, and sustained funding ref [39], ref [8].

A supplementary planning perspective is that implementation success depends not only on analytical sensitivity but also on governance. Effective programs link utilities, laboratories, epidemiologists, and decision-makers through predefined trigger frameworks and transparent communication of uncertainty. Experiences from national and regional monitoring efforts suggest that WBE is most actionable when results are rapidly translated into operational dashboards and paired with contextual metadata on population served and hydraulic conditions ref [3], ref [4], ref [9]. Thus, long-term feasibility rests on institutionalization: standard methods, interoperable data systems, and policy mechanisms that allow wastewater signals to inform routine urban health surveillance beyond the acute pandemic phase ref [39], ref [9].
